speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which relates to something that is the concern of all hon. members of parliament and to which the present government should give top priority, namely its relationship with parliament.
As hon. members know, I have several times during the course of this session sought to obtain information regarding the proposed legislation dealing with contributory or portable pensions. I have been told to contain myself, to be patient, because in due course the legislation would be presented to parliament.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in this morning's Toronto Globe and Mail there is a report of a speech made at Hamilton on Saturday by the Minister of National Health and Welfare in which the hon. lady is reported as having told the southern Ontario Liberal association that pension legislation would be introduced in this parliament, and in the course of her speech, as reported in the press, she gave fairly full details of that legislation. Some of the details are most welcome, but the point is that the parliament of Canada takes precedence over any party association.
I suggest that the Prime Minister should have a heart to heart talk with his cabinet ministers and tell them the facts of parliamentary life.

subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT AND MANPOWER DEVELOPMENT PROGRAM

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT AND MANPOWER DEVELOPMENT PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a statement on the major features of the employment and manpower development program of the government. This employment and manpower development program represents a balanced attack designed to reduce unemployment, promote manpower development and increase employment security particularly during the winter months. The government is convinced that we cannot continue to tolerate the excessively high levels of unemployment of recent years. Over the past five years unemployment has averaged 6.6 per cent of the labour force. During the winter the rate of unemployment has risen on the average to 10.1 per cent, while during the summer it has fallen to an average of 4.3 per cent of the labour force.
The stimulation of employment and the reduction of unemployment are major problems which the government is determined to tackle vigorously. To cope successfully with unemployment requires a variety of well integrated measures whose major objective is to step up our rate of economic

Labour Conditions
growth. This requires co-ordinated action on a wide front. An active employment and manpower development policy is an essential element of such a program. It is now widely recognized that the growth of our economy and the stimulation of employment are greatly facilitated by the improvement of the quality and skills of youth entering the labour force and on the adaptation of workers to constantly changing job requirements. The need for adaptation and retraining of our labour force is a consequence of a much stepped up rate of technological change in recent years. Disruptions in employment due to technological changes and seasonal fluctuations are of serious consequence for individual workers, their families, the industries of which they are members and the whole economy.
While some aspects of this employment and manpower development program are naturally related to measures introduced by the former government-and in this connection I wish to acknowledge the work of my predecessor-this program represents a new and distinctive approach. One of the new elements is the fact that the various measures are being put forward as a co-ordinated and balanced program rather than as a series of disconnected or separate efforts. In this way a more positive and vigorous attack can be mounted in co-operation with other federal and provincial government agencies, employer organizations, unions and all other groups in seeking solutions to the present employment and manpower problems facing us. This manpower program is designed to deal with unemployment, training and employment security.
The measures that will be introduced will deal with either one of these objectives or with all of them combined. Some of these measures will be of a short run nature; others are designed to deal with longer run problems. I shall now set forth briefly the steps that will be taken at this time in the implementation of this new employment and manpower development program.
1. Training of the unemployed.
In order to step up the training of unemployed workers of all ages the government will introduce an amendment to the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act to increase the contribution to the provinces of the cost of provincial training allowances to unemployed persons from 75 per cent to 90 per cent. At the present time we have the anomaly in this country of high unemployment and shortages of skills. By making a larger contribution to the provincial costs for providing training allowances for those unemployed workers who would benefit from

training, the provinces will be able to release more funds to support additional training programs.
2.	Training of employed workers.
To stimulate training in industry, the government will introduce an amendment to the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act to provide for an increase in the federal contribution toward the provincial costs of training in industry from 50 per cent to 75 per cent. This will be done in the case of programs of basic training for skill development, apprenticeship and the retraining of workers who may become subject to displacement as a result of technological and industrial changes.
3.	Re-employment of older workers.
In order to assist older persons who have been unemployed for a long time, steps will be taken to encourage their re-entry into employment along with the provision of appropriate training or other programs. A further announcement on this point will be made in a few days.
4.	Capital assistance for technical training facilities.
An amendment will be introduced to provide for the continuation of the 75 per cent federal contribution under the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act to capital expenditures incurred by the province on training facilities beyond March 31, 1963. The contribution at this 75 per cent level will be continued up to a specified total for each province. When provinces have reached this total level, the federal contribution will continue at 50 per cent until the expiry of the agreement. This will allow provinces to share in the provision for capital facilities to an equal extent and will at the same time give them more time to put these training facilities into place.
5.	Technological change and manpower development.
To assist labour and management to meet the employment problems caused by technological and other industrial changes, a manpower consultative or development service will be set up in the Department of Labour. This service will help develop programs designed to promote greater employment security. Provision will also be made for financial assistance to employers and unions for research on manpower development in advance of technological changes. In addition, a re-employment incentive will be provided to employers and the provinces to help workers and their dependants displaced by industrial change.

6.	Promotion of winter house building.
In order to stimulate employment in the construction of houses during the winter months, a winter house building incentive will be introduced. This incentive will consist of a direct payment of $500 to the first purchaser or owner of a house substantially built during the four winter months, December through March inclusive. This incentive will assist not only the purchasers of needed houses but will increase employment substantially during the winter months. It will also increase total employment through stimulating the housing and allied industries.
The program will be tried out during the coming winter. Its effects can then be evaluated in the light of the experience gained and the need for additional winter employment.
7.	Supplementary federal government winter construction.
In order to create greater employment opportunities during the coming winter in designated areas, certain federal government construction projects for which funds are not now provided in the estimates will be brought forward.
8.	Extension of municipal winter works incentive program.
The municipal winter works incentive program can be expected to do a more effective job in creating additional winter employment as a result of the municipal development loan fund which has already been announced.
Changes designed to increase further the effectiveness of the municipal works incentive program will also be made.
The ceiling on the federal incentive payment for buildings and major renovations will be increased from $50,000 to $100,000 to assist municipalities to plan the inclusion of larger buildings in the program.
The incentive payment will be increased from 50 per cent to 60 per cent of payroll expenditures for municipalities in designated areas to encourage a higher level of winter employment in those areas.
In recent years the municipal winter works incentive program has run over a period of seven and one half months. Even the Canadian winter does not last that long. This program was originally designed to concentrate additional employment in the winter months. The program this year will operate from November 1 to April 30 inclusive, in the full expectation that just as much or more work can be done to better effect in this shorter period of time.
Labour Conditions
To further this objective, the program is being announced at this early date so that municipalities will be enabled to advance their planning for next winter as much as possible.
9.	Strengthening personnel resources.
The government will take steps to strengthen the personnel resources of the agencies responsible for the administration of these manpower programs. These include various branches of the Department of Labour and the national employment service. The role of the national employment service is of fundamental importance in the effective operation of the labour market and in administering many of the manpower programs of the Department of Labour in an integrated way. In addition, we know far too little about the real nature of many of the complex manpower problems facing us in these areas. We intend to investigate these problems in depth.
As hon. members will appreciate, this is a many sided program. It will stimulate employment particularly during the winter months when it is most needed. It will expand substantially the training of the unemployed. It will help raise the general educational level of employed workers, increase apprenticeship programs, promote the re-employment of older workers and provide training for those subject to displacement. It will encourage planning by labour and management in advance of technological change, and programs for greater employment security. It will enable the provinces to continue the capital program for training facilities by extending the 75 per cent federal contribution. It will provide for much needed staff resources to meet these objectives. Finally, it will provide for the development of a well co-ordinated, balanced, and active employment and manpower development program.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the problem of unemployment is one that has had the attention of governments in the western world particularly during the last few years when, in consequence of automation, and so far as our own country is concerned a continuation of inclement winter conditions, unemployment has been a continuing source of difficulty and concern to successive governments.
In so far as the program which has been placed before the house by the Minister of Labour is concerned, I thank him for his reference to his predecessor, the former minister of labour. In the course of his concluding remarks he said that this would be the co-ordination, as it were, of various plans to meet this very important problem. I would

Labour Conditions
point out that a major portion of the co-ordination, outside of the housing plan, consists of an alteration of the percentage to be paid to the provinces, the increase in one case being, if I took it down correctly, from 75 per cent to 90 per cent in training unemployed, and in another from 50 per cent to 75 per cent in training employed workers. I would be interested to know, in view of the strong statements made by the Prime Minister during the election campaign, whether this is one sharing program which is going to be acceptable to each and all of the provinces, for after all it was said over and over again that the day of sharing programs was over. Instead of it being over, it is being increased in this case.
As far as training of men and women is concerned to meet the technological changes of today, we made very great advances in this regard. We made available some $300 million for technical education. I am glad that this is going to be continued. There is no real expansion in this regard. From what I have been able to ascertain from endeavouring to follow the hon. gentleman, as far as re-employment of old workers is concerned, and the manpower and consultant service, these plans were ours and were available to parliament from September last until February 5, but we were unable to get them before the house at the time owing to the attitude taken by the then opposition, the government of today. However, we welcome the conversion on the part of the government to the plan which we had available and ready for parliament.
In so far as the program to encourage house building in the winter is concerned, on its face it looks like quite an unusual plan in that it makes it possible for the first purchaser to receive a credit of $500 on the house. That plan, of course, is subject to one general criticism, namely that it is discriminatory. It only applies to those who will be purchasing houses to be proceeded with in the winter of 1963-64.
Generally I think the ideas as to housing will be acceptable. I am surprised that there has been a change on the part of the government from the attitude taken by the government which I had the honour to lead, in that the present government has stated in advance that there will be no extension beyond April 30 for the winter works program. I would say to the minister that while theoretically this sounds well, I think he will find in the light of experience that municipalities by about the first of March next will be placing before the government projects that they have in mind and will be asking for an extension, and I am sure that at that time the pressure on the government to extend the period of time will bring about a condition similar to that which prevailed under the former government.
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
Anything that can be done by way of correlation or novel legislation to meet the problem of unemployment will always receive the support of this party and the official opposition. I would point out that many of these plans have been placed before the people of the United States. I recall well the campaign of 1960 in the United States when there was a promise on the part of the Democratic party as to what they were going to do to meet the problem of unemployment. One just has to look at the record week by week to know that unemployment is not being decreased in the United States.
As far as our country is concerned, the best advice we had was that as a result of the policies we had placed on the statute books and the practices applied by the Department of Labour there would be a very substantial reduction in the rate of unemployment by this summer even compared with last summer, and that in the expanding economy which we left to the present government this problem was rapidly approaching the point where a solution to the difficulty would certainly be achieved. Anything that will bring about the acceleration of that hope will certainly receive our support.
It is impossible to refer one by one to the matters raised by the Minister of Labour, but I say this. Three of them are rehashes, two of them were available, and the other two are of doubtful application.

Mr. Speaker, we welcome the statement that has been made by the Minister of Labour. I think perhaps what we like best about it is the recognition implicit in the
Labour Conditions
statement that there is no one simple answer to the problem of unemployment, but rather that it has to be attacked on every possible front. I am glad to note the number of steps the Minister of Labour has suggested, some of which are a continuation of policies proposed by previous governments and some of which are new. We earnestly hope that these and other steps will be taken and will be pursued so that we will really get rid of unemployment.
I am afraid that we in this corner of the house do not agree with the comment made by the Leader of the Opposition to the effect that under his government the solution of the unemployment problem had just about been achieved. As long as we have unemployment of the order of 5 per cent or 6 per cent or more of the working population there is no point in talking about the solution of the unemployment problem being just around the corner. We do not claim that we in this corner are alone in this, but we feel that we must keep working on this problem of unemployment until we lick it completely. They have come close to licking it in other countries, in countries with climates similar to ours, and we see no reason why we should not pursue this matter until we have unemployment down to something less than 1 per cent of our working population.
We agree with the statement made by the hon. member for Lake St. John as to the importance of the municipal development and loan fund which the present government has proposed. We were glad the Minister of Labour mentioned it in his remarks. We would emphasize the point that if the winter works program is to be as effective as it could be it will have to be dovetailed into the activities under the municipal development and loan fund. We all recognize that this is one of the places where we can most quickly get the economy rolling-it seems to me I have heard that phrase somewhere-in terms of providing employment for those who need it.
We welcome the various references to housing. It is still our view that both in the immediate future and over the long run, one way in which to do a real job in terms of reducing unemployment is to make a massive attack on the housing problem in this country. Far too many Canadian people still live in substandard dwellings in communities which lack the kind of conveniences and the kind of organization that we could have in this day and age.
While we welcome the suggestions that have been made in respect of new housing, we would like to put in a word for the rehabilitation of older dwellings. There are many dwellings in this country that should be torn down. However, there are many older

Labour Conditions
ones that could be rehabilitated, and work on them in the winter months would not only be beneficial in what it would do to those dwellings but would provide employment. We hope that, amongst other things, the Minister of Labour and the government will consider this aspect.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, what pleased us most in the minister's statement was the recognition that unemployment must be attacked from every possible angle; training, tackling the problems of automation, over-all planning, providing the necessary means for moving people about from job to job, incentives, taxation and fiscal policy, aid to municipalities, and consideration of the weather we have in this country. I was glad to learn, coming as I do from Winnipeg, that we have only seven and a half months of winter in this country. Maybe it is just that it does not always seem that way in Winnipeg.
I was glad to hear from the minister recognition that this was a problem of many parts. We hope that every effort will be made by the government, and if it does it will have the support of the whole house as it seeks really to lick the problem of unemployment in Canada.

subtopic: NORTH PACIFIC TREATY-STATEMENT ON MEETINGS IN WASHINGTON

speakeroldname: Hon. H. J. Robichaud (Minister of Fisheries):
subtopic: NORTH PACIFIC TREATY-STATEMENT ON MEETINGS IN WASHINGTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday last I advised the house that I would make a statement today on the series of meetings which are now taking place in Washington, and which opened last Thursday, to review the provisions of the north Pacific treaty.
In 1952 Canada, Japan and the United States entered into a treaty, the international north Pacific fisheries convention, the principal basis of which was the abstention principle. Under this principle it was agreed that any stocks of fish which are fully utilized by any one or more of the participating countries, and which are under regulation based on scientific investigation, will continue to be exploited only by the countries which have developed those fisheries to their full exploitation. Also any country which had not, for 25 years preceding the entry into force of the convention, exploited such stocks of fish agreed voluntarily to abstain from fishing such stocks.
Under this principle Japan, which had never participated in the exploitation of salmon,

halibut and herring fisheries of North American origin, agreed to continue abstaining from fishing these stocks. Canada, which had never exploited stocks of salmon in the Bering sea, also agreed to abstain from fishing those stocks.
The treaty was made for a period of 10 years following its ratification on June 12, 1953, after which time any of the parties to the convention could terminate the convention by giving 12 months notice. Before the expiration of the 10 year period this June Japan had requested that the three countries enter into discussions to review the convention and to consider the possibility of revisions.
The three parties met on Thursday of last week at the opening session in Washington, and stated their positions. From the statements made it is evident that the three parties are agreed on the fact that a treaty is needed for the protection of the fishing resources of the north Pacific. The differences between the parties are as to the kind of treaty that would give this protection. The Japanese position was stated by the Japanese chairman of the delegation, Mr. Masayoshi Ito, as follows:
The implementation of the convention for 10 years has revealed that the formula of abstention contains in itself a number of difficult problems such as the difficulty of proving the existence of the conditions for abstention.
Therefore, the government of Japan hopes to conclude, in place of the present convention which will shortly have run its initial ten year period, a new convention the objective of which is to ensure the rational conservation and exploitation of the fishery resources of the north Pacific ocean by co-operation between our three countries, Canada, the United States and Japan.
Japan is heavily dependant on fishery resources so that the conservation of resources is a matter of greatest concern to us. The government of Japan, while urging the discard of the formula of abstention, has no wish adversely to affect fishery resources and is prepared to give due consideration to the past efforts of the countries concerned for the conservation of those resources.
Secretary of the Interior Stewart L. Udall expressed the views of the United States government and its delegation as follows:
It is our view in the United States that the convention has served well as a mechanism for the solution of common fishery problems and in so doing has contributed substantially to a pattern of harmonious relations among the three governments.
Further on he said:
In short, we are convinced of the fundamental value of the principle of abstention for the solution of what are today unique fishery problems, but problems which may in the future be all too common.
We are strengthened in our conviction by the manner in which this convention has served the three governments during the past 10 years. None of the governments has found in the functioning of the convention all that it might have hoped for. Japanese fishermen find defects in the convention, and so do Canadian and American fishermen. But, within its framework it has been possible for the three national fishing industries to prosper.
North Pacific Treaty
I shall quote two paragraphs of what I said, speaking for the Canadian delegation:
Speaking for my country, I may say that the government is deeply conscious of the arduous work put in by the commission to demonstrate that the principles on which the international north Pacific fisheries convention is founded are sound. The abstention principle, on which the convention is based, is meant to cover a unique situation to protect certain fisheries which without it could not long survive.
Further on I said:
One of the emerging problems in conservation of sea fisheries, which requires an urgent solution, is the intermingling of various stocks of fish. One state may be interested in exploiting a certain stock of fish which may be intermingled with a stock or stocks of fish which another state may be desirous of exploiting in the same region. This probably is the knottiest problem to be resolved in the fisheries of the north Pacific.
I concluded with the following remarks:
In closing I express the hope that your deliberations will be successful, and successful they must be if we want to preserve the rich resources of our north Pacific high seas for the common benefit of future generations of our respective countries.
Requests for the calling back of the Canadian delegation to Ottawa, as well as accusations against the Japanese of taking advantage of the weak kneed, unprincipled approach displayed by the Canadian government, its fisheries department and its hand picked puppets, are having no other effect than to undermine and render more difficult the progress and success of the present negotiations. I want to state that we have full confidence in the departmental officials, the scientists, the members of the north Pacific commission, and the technical advisers who form part of the Canadian delegation. Their competence and ability are well known throughout the Canadian fisheries industry. In concluding I must add that the Canadian delegation has the full support and confidence of the Fisheries Council of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the official opposition I want to say that we welcome this interim report on the negotiations now going on at Washington on the question of modifications to the international north Pacific fisheries treaty. I feel, and I think the minister will agree with me, that one of the most important international problems which will develop in the years ahead is a rational and reasonable method of deciding jurisdiction over and ownership of resources of the high seas so they can be divided equally among the nations which are most entitled to them.
I also, of course, have every confidence in the officials and fishery experts of this country. They are among the best in the world, and I know they will serve our country well in Washington. The most important

North Pacific Treaty
responsibility resting on the Canadian delegation is to assure for Canadians the harvesting of fishery resources that are developing, and that have been developed over the years, as a result of conservation and other measures taken by Canada, jointly with the United States in most cases. The fishery resources which exist are due mainly to the fact that Canada has abstained from hydro developments and various other projects which would endanger the survival of present fish stocks.
I have nothing else to add at the moment, but we will look forward with interest to further reports.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we also appreciate this interim report regarding the discussions that are currently proceeding in Washington, and we note that the minister has indicated that each of the three nations concerned has indicated its recognition of the fact that the commission and the treaty have worked very successfully down through the years.
I might say there is a great deal of concern among fishermen in British Columbia areas regarding some of the factors involved; and I believe they had a right to be concerned when the announcement was made that the Japanese were requesting, or demanding, the complete elimination of the abstention principle. That is a feature which has been recognized as very worth while and very important down through the years. When the fishermen heard this, of course they were very perturbed about this request.
We also noted what the minister said relative to the confidence the government has in those who are carrying on the negotiations. Unfortunately the minister has not been able to develop an attitude of confidence on the part of the fishermen toward himself and his department because of some of the activities that have taken place very recently. Requests have been made for an immediate meeting of the marine and fisheries committee to discuss some of the problems, but this has not as yet been agreed to. I think these requests are very locigal, and that the fishermen themselves ought to have adequate opportunity to present their views and make known their ideas relative to these various matters in connection with the international north Pacific fisheries treaty. There is the feeling that this treaty ought to be expanded. There is also the suggestion that at least some meetings ought to be held in the west coast area in order to facilitate the representations that are required in this connection.
We do urge once again, Mr. Speaker, that in all these discussions and deliberations this thought must be kept in mind; that our fisheries must be preserved and that Canadian

interests must be maintained. There must also be a recognition of the fact that as far as some of the species of fish are concerned, they are Canadian products; that even though they may go far out into the ocean their conservation is connected with the Canadian fisheries and therefore Canadian fishermen ought to be considered in these matters.
So we welcome this interim report, Mr. Speaker, and will await further reports from time to time.

subtopic: NORTH PACIFIC TREATY-STATEMENT ON MEETINGS IN WASHINGTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in replying to the minister's statement I would like to say that we of the New Democratic party still believe, despite his optimistic views, that the number and gravity of the problems facing the fishing industry of Canada are such as to make the immediate establishment of the standing committee of the house on marine and fisheries essential. Particularly in regard to the north Pacific is this the case. We remain of the opinion that this government's sudden implementation of the controversial recommendation of the north Pacific fisheries commission extending new rights to Japan last month should first have been referred to the house committee, with time and opportunity given for all sections of the industry, and the British Columbia government, to make their representations.
As we pointed out then and repeat now, the result of the concessions made to Japan in herring and halibut have led to new demands by Japan at Washington which may jeopardize the British Columbia fishing industry. As an indication of the growth of Japanese activities, figures show a marked decline in the B.C. sockeye catch while a marked increase has taken place in the Japanese high seas sockeye catch. Using statistics from the Canadian Department of Fisheries for the B.C. catch, and from the Pacific Fisherman Year Book for the Japanese catch, we find that a decline in the B.C. sockeye catch has taken place from an annual average catch of 5,478,000 fish during the period 1951 to 1954 to an annual average catch of 3,536,000 fish during the period 1959 to 1962. At the same time the Japanese high seas sockeye catch has risen from an annual average of 2 million in the first five year period mentioned to 12 million in the second. We believe that a thoroughgoing overhaul of the existing north Pacific fisheries treaty is needed and that Canada should interest herself in making the present three power treaty-which I might almost say divides Canada, the United States and Japan-into a four-power treaty, bringing in Russia, the other north Pacific power, and making her subject to regulation.

We press in this regard for the immediate setting up of the House of Commons standing committee on marine and fisheries and for the inclusion in its deliberations, and those going on at Washington, of all sections of the fisheries industry; and in respect of British Columbia problems we ask that the views of the British Columbia government also be taken into consideration.

It has now been announced that agreement has been reached to hold further talks in Moscow, probably in July. It is our understanding that these talks will not be at the foreign minister or head of government level, but will involve senior representatives of the three countries. President Kennedy has also stated that the United States will refrain from atmospheric nuclear tests as long as other states do not test in the atmosphere.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice, notice of which I sent to him this morning. In view of the government's announcement that legislation will shortly be introduced to validate the taxation imposed by order in council last June 24, will the Minister of Justice take steps to have a revision made of the legal opinion given to the House of Commons last session, in a sessional paper laid on the table of the house, to the effect that the provisions of the surcharge on imports order were not inconsistent with the purposes and provisions of the Canadian Bill of Rights?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: OPINION AS TO CONSISTENCY WITH BILL OF RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to the hon. gentleman for sending me notice of his question. The answer is that section 3 of the Canadian Bill of Rights requires the Minister of Justice, in accordance with regulations, to examine draft regulations and bills introduced in the House of Commons in order to ascertain whether they are inconsistent with the bill of rights, and the minister is required to report any such inconsistency to the House of Commons.

Under the regulations, the bills and regulations are examined by the deputy minister and he attaches his certificate, as required by the regulations, that they have been examined in accordance with the provisions of the bill of rights. The certificate does not state whether or not they are inconsistent with the bill of rights. Any representations the deputy might have to make would be made to the minister for his consideration in forming his opinion. There was no report to the minister from the deputy minister on the bill of rights in connection with the surcharge order.
In the present case the certificate did not, as suggested by the question, indicate approval so far as the bill of rights was concerned; it merely stated that the surcharge order had been examined. This is a statement of fact, and there is therefore nothing to revise.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: OPINION AS TO CONSISTENCY WITH BILL OF RIGHTS
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Do I take it from what the minister says that the signature of the deputy minister of justice on these hundreds of proposed bills and proposed regulations really has no meaning at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: OPINION AS TO CONSISTENCY WITH BILL OF RIGHTS
speechtext: I would not say it has no meaning at all. It has this meaning, that in so far as parliament is concerned there is no inconsistency in these bills or regulations. It is up to parliament to determine what the position may be. For instance, the Minister of Justice could not be expected to issue a certificate to parliament that a measure is consistent with the bill of rights. This would be a matter for parliament in the first instance, and for the courts in the last instance. What the Minister of Justice might reasonably be expected to do is draw to the attention of the house any provisions that, in his judgment, do offend the bill of rights. The house could then take such action as it sees fit.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: OPINION AS TO CONSISTENCY WITH BILL OF RIGHTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask a further supplementary question. In view of the minister's statement that the signature of the deputy minister on this certificate means that there is nothing objectionable in the light of the bill of rights, does the minister not now think that the opinion implied in this case should be revised, in view of the uncertainty that has arisen about this order in council?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week the hon. member for Churchill asked a question of the Secretary of State for External Affairs with regard to U.S. rocket testing at Fort Churchill. Rocket launchings at the research range at Fort Churchill have only recently been resumed, following the restoration of research facilities destroyed by fire early in 1961. These launchings are conducted at Fort Churchill under an agreement made between the governments of Canada and the United States in 1960.
The experiments consist of two main types, as follows: (a) the launching of high altitude rockets to obtain measurements of the upper atmosphere. These research projects are designed and conducted by governmental research agencies and universities of Canada and the United States; and (b) the launching for test purposes of rockets being developed for use in upper atmosphere research. This is a Canadian program in entirety.
The construction and restoration program resulting from the fire is expected to be completed by midsummer, to accommodate a total of about 70 high altitude rockets to be launched in the period July 1, 1963 to June 30, 1964. This total includes six Canadian rockets to be launched for flight test purposes. It is expected that in future years operations will be on a similar scale.

The house resumed, from Friday, June 7, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Pearson-Mr. Lamoureux in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure (a) to establish a department of industry to be presided over by a minister of industry who shall be appointed under the Great Seal of Canada, to authorize the appointment of a deputy minister by the governor in council and to provide for the appointment to the department on a temporary basis of persons having special knowledge of manufacturing industries to assist in the work of the department; (b) to provide for the establishment under the direction of the minister of an area development agency and to provide for the appointment of a commissioner and a deputy commissioner for area development; and (c) to make a consequential amendment to the Salaries Act to provide a salary for the minister.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

Mr. Chairman, on Friday afternoon we saw a great example of cooperation between the opposition parties and
10,	1983
Establishment of Industry Department the government in proceeding with legislation, and possibly because of the speed with which we were operating I spoke in more general terms than I otherwise would have in dealing with this specific resolution. Now, in the few minutes left to me perhaps I can pinpoint and bring into focus the remarks I made at that time.
We are dealing with a resolution which envisages the division of the Department of Trade and Commerce into two departments, one of which will be a department of industry and the other which may retain the name trade and commerce. The reason given for this proposal is the necessity of emphasizing the development of industry in Canada. I want to make it very plain, Mr. Chairman, that we of the official opposition are fully in accord with the government in stressing the importance of developing industry in every way, shape and form.
The other afternoon the Prime Minister referred to the employment which would flow from an increase in secondary industry. With that we are also fully in accord. There is no doubt that secondary industry must develop if we are going to provide the employment which the country requires, but I question the necessity of dividing the department into two compartments in order to place a greater emphasis on the development of industry.
I suggested on Friday, and I repeat now, that such a division is not necessary, and the justification for that stand lies in the record of what the Department of Trade and Commerce has done during the last few years in developing secondary industry. In the few minutes left to me I am not going to take time to put the figures on the record, showing the tremendous development which did take place over the last few years in the manufacture of cars and the increase in steel production. There was an increase in almost every facet of our industrial life, and that in itself is an answer to the argument that the department must be divided in order to achieve greater efficiency. In fact I suggest that this division will increase bureaucracy and reduce efficiency, rather than increase it.
It may well be that the name of the department should be changed from trade and commerce to trade and industry, or even industry and trade, because due recognition must be paid to the important part industry has to play in the development of our country. However I do not think that will be accomplished by putting trade and industry in two watertight compartments. As I asked the other day, where does industry stop and trade begin? If one reads the remarks of the

Establishment of Industry Department Prime Minister in introducing this resolution on Friday the answer to that question is found there.
As recorded at page 802 of Hansard for June 7 the Prime Minister referred to the fact that the resolution of our problems did not lie in an increase in protection, with which I agree entirely. I shall not quote him exactly but hon. members will find his remarks at pages 802 and 803 of Hansard, where he said that if industry were to develop it would be necessary to increase our trade, and that we would have to seek out markets in the new countries of the world. Certainly that is true. There is no use in manufacturing goods unless they are sold; and I suggest again, sir, that the arguments made by the Prime Minister on Friday afternoon in dealing at some length with markets around the world-Asia, Africa, South America; he mentioned them all-show a good reason why we should maintain trade and industry working together, in developing manufacturing on the one hand and selling on the other, rather than put them into two separate, watertight compartments.
What will we have after these measures are put through, presuming they are implemented? On Friday afternoon we passed a resolution setting up the economic council. This, as I think I said the other day, will come, presumably, judging from press reports I have read-and I think perhaps it is in the speech from the throne, although I am not sure of that. It is apparently the intention of the government to have this economic council come under the aegis, the care, the eye of the President of the Privy Council. This is the body which is going to give advice on the development of the economy of this country; it will be done under the President of the Privy Council.
If the legislation based on this resolution is adopted we will have a minister of industry on the one side of the clock, if you like; we will have a minister of trade on the other side, and down at the bottom we will have the Minister of Finance who is responsible for the fiscal and financial policies of this country. If that is not a cumbersome practice to follow, Mr. Chairman, I would like to know what is. I do not know how we will get efficiency in the development of trade and commerce and the economic development of this country when we have not only a bifocal, but something like the Irishman's clock. When asked how it operated, because no one could understand it, the Irishman said, "When the hands point at nine and the clock strikes seven, then I know it will be half past eleven". That is roughly the Irishman's clock which is being created by this


government in its attempt to streamline and develop the economy of this country.
One could go on at length with that matter, Mr. Chairman, but I do not propose to do so. I want to refer to one other matter in this connection. The Prime Minister said this is going to be a merger, a common law marriage or alliance of some kind, between the new department of industry and the old Department of Defence Production. We will have the minister who is now responsible for the Department of Defence Production being responsible not only for that but for the department of industry also. Then off in one corner, when he gets time to look at it, I take it we are going to have an organization for the development of areas where unemployment exists. We are going to have the minister looking after that also. I wonder just how much time the Minister of Defence Production is going to have to give to this emerging, most important department of industry.
We listened to the Minister of Defence Production when he came back from Washington the other day. I noticed that he almost had a prayer on his lips when he was asked whether he thought sales of defence equipment to the United States could increase. I think he dealt with the matter frankly and said there would be difficulties in that connection. He also pointed out that there would have to be increased purchases from the United States if increased sales were to take place, because Canada is not the only country in the world which from time to time has suffered or is suffering from a balance of payments problem. He has a real problem in that connection, and I think there will be some anxiety on the part of those who were possibly looking forward to the creation of a department of industry, as to which is going to be the tail and which is going to be the dog in the new set-up which is envisioned in this measure. We not only have the four facets of it, but we have sleeping under the same blanket, somehow or other, an uneasy alliance. The Department of Defence Production and the problems which can arise I think are going to be such that one cannot expect too much development in the department of industry.
These are matters which, as I said, are the responsibility of the government. As far as we of the opposition are concerned, naturally we are waiting for the bill. When the bill is before us we can discuss its terms at greater length and see what the government has in mind with respect to it, and we will then be in a position to decide what action we shall take clause by clause or on the bill as a whole. I simply repeat, Mr. Chairman, that I do not think this will promote the efficiency of the department and it will not accomplish

the very laudable ends which the Prime Minister specified in his speech. I am wondering how many of these things were born during the times of stress and strain when one was flitting from one place to another during an election campaign and it was necessary or thought advisable to make pledges which now, in the cold light of reason, may seem rather awkward or cumbersome to carry out. If that should be the case, I would suggest to the government that they reconsider this measure before they go further with it.

Mr. Chairman, the remarks of the genial Prime Minister prompt me to rise in my place and speak this afternoon on this resolution, chiefly because I differ greatly with him in his approach to the basic problem, which is unemployment. I refer to unemployment because of the remarks of the Prime Minister to which I should like to refer in order to point out exactly what 1 mean. As reported at page 802 of Hansard he said this:
What. .. are to be the sources of the new wealth and employment which Canada needs? Where are we going to provide the jobs for the 250,000 young people by which our labour force is going to increase in each of the next few years?
I agree with the Prime Minister that this is a problem, but I am saying that I do not agree with the approach to the problem and the purpose of industry as outlined by his remarks. Further on he said:
Where will we find, in addition, the new jobs that are needed to keep pace with automation and other technological changes-
Then further on:
-manufacturing industry, secondary industry, is the source from which the new wealth and the new employment must largely come.
These statements indicate to me that the purpose behind this new ministry is to get industry going for the providing of jobs. I do not think that is the purpose of industry. The purpose of industry, to my mind, is solely to produce goods and provide services. To that end industry is bent to use all the means at its disposal in order to produce the greatest amount of goods and services at the least cost; in other words, there is keen competition. I notice, too, that the Prime Minister has related the bringing in of this resolution to establish a ministry of trade with the measure relating to the Canadian economic council which was previously passed by this house. I think if he had related it to the proposed municipal development fund in connection with providing job opportunities we would be far, far in advance of where we will be if we take the stand the Prime Minister has taken here in introducing a measure for the establishment of this new ministry. I find that in following the reasoning of the
Establishment of Industry Department Prime Minister throughout he has stepped very gingerly into the political field of relations between the provinces and the federal government when he says that this will in no way lessen or interfere with provincial responsibilities, and the new federal department will not in any way create new federal responsibilities.
In this connection I should like to suggest to the Prime Minister that if his thinking in connection with this ministry were related to the municipal development fund, we would be getting down to a solid foundation from which we could build. To my mind the business of expecting industry to provide jobs by the production of goods and services, which may or may not be sold, is a horse and buggy way of trying to solve a very, very acute problem. I believe we must get to the root of this problem. We must bring about employment in such a way that the price of the product does not include the cost of creating these new opportunities. What better way could be found of doing this than through a municipal development fund and the public works which would be embarked on as this fund begins to operate?
I hope that during the committee stage some consideration will be given to where this money is coming from, but I shall not deal with that aspect of the subject now. The jobs which will be created as a result of the use of the municipal development fund will create, in turn, a market for goods and services where there is no market today. Putting men to work will create a market, and industry will respond, as it always has responded to new markets. As far as Canada is concerned, there is no such thing as a foreign market. There is only trade. We send something out of Canada, and countries abroad send something back. We have nothing in the way of a market, in reality. If, then, our market is a domestic market, we have to develop that market here. This fund will create a climate in which industry can make progress. Then industry, itself, in meeting the demands of the market, will be able to employ more people who will, in turn, require more goods and services-a snowball effect which will, as it develops, solve to a great extent the problem of unemployment, possibly even to the extent suggested by the Prime Minister, by bringing about a situation in which we can encourage more people to enter Canada from countries outside by way of a revived immigration program. We need such a development badly in Canada today, because a greater population would reduce the per capita cost of many large scale undertakings including, for example, the railways. One of our problems in Canada today is that we have two railways across the length and

Establishment of Industry Department breadth of the country and a sparse population to support their operation. The result is a high charge falling on the individual. In addition, an increase in our population, both naturally and as a result of increased immigration, would stimulate the production of goods and services.
Today we face a serious situation in the distressed areas of Canada. The thought which is embodied in this legislation is, apparently, that such areas will become the targets, as it were, of the new ministry which is to be created along with the economic council. I say that the increased population which will result if we start at the right place and follow correct policies will bring about a much improved situation as far as these depressed areas are concerned. This will come about automatically because of the new markets which will spring up in the distressed areas as a result of the growth in the population.
I should like to leave this thought with the Prime Minister, that we should seriously consider bringing about, through the municipal development fund, a situation in which an expansion in industry would come about naturally on the basis of supply and demand. I hope that before the present debate is over other hon. members will spend some time discussing this particular point, because I believe that the provision of incentives to industry to produce goods as a means of producing jobs is not the way to solve this problem. The answer lies in creating, through financial and other means, a climate in which the people of Canada can buy back what they themselves produce. I think the answer lies in the people's ability to buy back their own production. If we could bring such a situation about, I am sure a far better and sounder economy would be ours.

In speaking to the resolution at this stage I should like to say that we have examined the resolution and the Prime Minister's speech in some detail. While we are anxious to support any measures which will be beneficial to industry in Canada generally, both the resolution and the speech itself raise problems in our minds, and we should like to put forward certain questions in the hope that the government might elaborate on these points when the bill comes up for second reading. We do not wish to spend very much time on the resolution; we want to have the bill before us so that we may examine it in detail.
The first question I wish to put to the government is this: what exactly is being created by this resolution? Is it another government department with the usual limited statutory authority, or is the government

endeavouring to create a planning instrument designed to carry out the program and advice of the economic council of Canada? Examination of the Prime Minister's speech on this subject does not make this distinction clear. As reported on page 801 of Hansard, the right hon. gentleman said:
The point and purpose of the department of industry which it is proposed to set up will be to assist in transmitting these various ideas into effective action.
He was referring to the ideas of the economic council. Then, further on, as reported on page 802, he said:
The bill... is one to create a department which will be for the manufacturing industry what the Department of Agriculture is for farmers.
With respect, it seems to me one cannot have both. If we are creating another department of government it is one which will surely be equal with the other departments, without power to encroach upon the preserves of those other departments or in any way to co-ordinate the work of such important ministries as those of trade and commerce, labour and finance. On the other hand, if what we are attempting to create is a planning agency to carry out the programs and intentions of the economic council, surely this new department will need the very powers I have mentioned-power to co-ordinate the work of other departments, to review their activities and draw those activities together.
It seems to me, then, that it is essential at this stage to know whether we are merely creating another department of government or whether we are attempting, as the Prime Minister seemed to suggest, to create an agency which would put into effective action the programs and policy of the economic council. If we are, in fact, creating an agency to carry out the ideas of that council, how is the department going to put into practice the advice of that council? Again, if we examine the speech made by the Prime Minister on the resolution, there is no definite indication of how this desirable end will be brought about. The right hon. gentleman's speech contained many phrases such as "to maintain close and direct contact with industry" and "to make sure that industry gets service from the government". There is this further expression: "a department to which manufacturers can come to find out what is going on, to get advice and help in their problems", and this further one: "to provide a focal point". To take these phrases together seems to indicate that you are building essentially an advisory assistance bureau chiefly concerned with making information available to industry in this country and hoping it will act upon your recommendations. Then at another point in his speech in referring to the department of

industry the Prime Minister goes on to say- and this to me is the more interesting part- that it will be concerned with translating into specifics the more general ideas about economic growth generated in the economic council. Then at another point he said that it will be concerned with the building rather than the blueprints of the expanding economy.
I should like to ask the government, what powers is this agency to have so that it can co-ordinate the work of the various departments? If it is going to carry out the views and ideas of the economic council, what will be its relationship to, and power over, such agencies as the economic council, the Atlantic development board, the municipal loan fund, the proposed Canadian development corporation, the national productivity council, other departments of government and crown agencies? If it is going to have any degree of responsibility for the co-ordination of all of these, as it would have to do, to carry out any sort of economic plan, we should like to hear on second reading what proposed powers this agency is to receive from the government.
Mr. Chairman, the resolution and the speech accompanying it made special mention of the need to rely on manufacturing and secondary industry as our future source of growth of jobs. Does this mean that it will not concern itself with the wide area of the service industries which are the agencies in and the area of our economy which are growing in employment and are providing a large portion of our present jobs? We should like to know the relationship of this department to the whole service industry and the jobs it provides. We should also like to know what is the real purpose of this department. If its real purpose is to carry out the advice of the planning council, it will inevitably be driven into activity in the following fields: As I said, the co-ordination of all government departments; the co-ordination of other planning agencies and boards; the co-ordination of the work of our provincial and regional planning boards; the co-ordination of crown corporations; and, more importantly, the coordination of private industrial plans and controls over the amount and direction of private investment. We should like to know what is envisaged for this department of industry in these very important fields.
The reason why these questions should be answered, it seems to me, is in reference to the speech of the Prime Minister, when he discussed the objects of this department. As reported on page 803 of Hansard, he said:
Canada's need is for industries that will thrive in the modern world, industries that will fit into the new patterns of international trade which are now emerging and to which we will have to adapt ourselves.
Our special need in this country-and this applies to other highly developed countries-is to create
10, 1963	851
Establishment of Industry Department and expand the more sophisticated, the more complicated, if you like, kinds of industry producing goods which we both need ourselves and which we can sell to other countries.
Finally he said:
So the aim of the department we propose will not be to shelter or shore up weak, protected enterprises but to encourage and build up economic industries and to help industries adapt themselves-
Mr. Chairman, if taken literally that involves a very far reaching change in the industrial picture in Canada.
How is this department to do this? Suppose it does decide that there is a genuine need for a shift in investment from one industry to another, how is it going to accomplish this? What techniques and powers are going to be placed at its disposal? We know the tax incentives, while they have some value, are somewhat limited because of the reserves many of our Canadian industries have built up, which to some extent cushion them against this. Can we expect a program of adjustment and assistance in the event that this department decides to shift investment from one major sector to another? What advice about financial aid does it envisage giving to industries in this country?
Another question we would like to pose is: If this is just another government department, what is its purpose and what are its real objectives? It seems to me, with respect, that these answers are not adequately spelled out in the resolution or in the speech accompanying it. Is its object to increase the aggregate of investment and production? Is it to reduce imports and encourage the production of Canadian goods now imported? Is it to shift investment and production from certain channels to other channels in accordance with one over-all plan? The speech talks about an industry-by-industry study. What happens to these studies, once they are completed? What powers is the department going to have to ensure that they are actually implemented, once these studies have been made? The speech talks about building up economic industries rather than shoring up weak and protected ones. We should like to know how this is to be done and what powers over the shifting of investment are going to be made available to this new agency.
On the whole, in examining the presentation to date, Mr. Chairman, it seems that, despite the contradictions, this is intended to be a government department alone which will be investigatory in nature and advisory in character. If this is so, it seems to me that we are developing the worst of all possible worlds. Because we already have a multiplicity of boards and bodies, fact-gathering agencies and economy forecasting organizations in this country, and merely to add to
852	HOUSE OF
Establishment of Industry Department them another such agency without making some provision for this agency to co-ordinate the work of other government departments, other crown agencies and planning boards, is adding another voice to all those now crying out. What is really needed is some agency to draw together all of these organizations and to come up with a complete blueprint and then to have an agency with the machinery for seeing that this blueprint is carried out.
Mr. Chairman, in sitting down may I just re-emphasize our participation at this stage is largely for purposes of clarification. We should like to know what we are creating, whether just a government department or some agency to carry out the plans and progress of the economic council. What is it expected really to do, and what powers is it going to have, so that it can adequately carry out the responsibilities given to it? We emphasize again that it cannot do both. If you are going to have a government department, then you will have your statutory limitation on your activity, with no power to mix into other government departments. If, as indicated in the speech, this is an agency to carry out the plans of the economic council, then it will need an entirely different set of powers. Neither is such power indicated in the speech, nor is it made clear in the resolution. Therefore we hope that when this bill comes up for second reading we may have some answers to the problems I have mentioned today, so that we will be in a much better position to analyse it dhd give it the attention it merits, and to make a decision upon it.

Mr. Chairman, this resolution has a great deal of personal interest to me because one of the first private members' resolutions that I presented when I became a member of this house was concerned with the urgent necessity of the federal government taking some action which would encourage the diversification and the decentralization of industry. It seems to me that the resolution to set up a department of industry at present before the committee is going to have as its major function those purposes which we used to talk about back at the beginning of the decade of the fifties. At that time the government of the day was not very much concerned about the need for urgent action on these matters and it is somewhat encouraging to see that at this late date there is recognition that we do have fundamental problems with regard to scattering our industrial potential across the nation, and also encouraging its diversification.
As the Prime Minister indicated in introducing the resolution the other day, actually much of the action that has been needed in

this connection since world war II has already been taken and most of the machinery is already present within the various departments of government. As far as I can see from the very information that has been put before the committee, the new proposal is designed to co-ordinate the machinery already existing in the Department of Trade and Commerce, the Department of Defence Production and the Department of Finance. I immediately raise this question: Is the Department of Defence Production the one that is best suited to meet the problems that this house and the country have been dealing with over the past 15 to 20 years? As a matter of fact, the record of the Department of Defence Production in this regard has not been a very encouraging one in the past. One of the unfortunate developments that took place in the early 1950's was the elimination in the year 1953 of the small defence industry branch. Just at the time when provincial governments in particular were becoming concerned about the increasing concentration of industry in the two large provinces this action was taken by the Department of Defence Production, which has now been chosen as the most appropriate department to carry forward the very important functions of decentralization and diversification.
It was quite logical in those days to encourage the activities of a small defence industry branch because at that time industry in Canada was very largely organized around the defence needs of the nation. World war I and world war II were the two periods when Canada's industrial potential grew apace. At the end of world war II it was quite obvious that our industrial potential was very closely geared to the defence needs that had emerged during the crisis of the second world war, and our industry continued in this orientation after the end of world war II.
I think very serious thought should be given by the government with respect to whether the Department of Defence Production is the most appropriate department to carry out these important functions. The Prime Minister made the statement the other day that much of the machinery is already in operation. I agree with him completely that this is quite true. A brief recital of some of the things that have taken place in the past six years, for example, is indicative of this point. Within the Department of Trade and Commerce there has been an entirely new area of activity to cope with the important functions of diversifying and decentralizing industry. A small business branch was established, for example, and the industrial development bank was expanded. Here are two functions that are scattered in separate
IMr. Scott.]

departments, one in trade and commerce and the other in the Department of Finance.
Again, the Farm Credit Corporation has expanded its activities in the area of diversifying our economy. I would refer too, to the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act because ARDA, in addition to dealing with problems of fundamental changes in agriculture, is also designed to assist the Canadian economy to adapt to the rapid change toward an industrial and urbanized community. The very successful series of trade conferences that have been held in Canada during recent years have also made a tremendous contribution in dealing with one of the difficult areas of Canadian industrial potential, namely, a market for our expanding industrial production. The productivity council has fulfilled an excellent function. It is only nicely getting under way at this time, and it was designed to deal with two of our basic problems, the increasing of the productivity of Canadian industry and the matter of co-ordination between the various sectors of the Canadian economy. As I understand the situation, the productivity council will be superseded by the new economic council, and there is some question whether this is a wise development.
The very fact that so much of the machinery has been established within various branches of government raises the query whether it is necessary at this time to establish a separate department of industry. Is the problem not one more of intragovernmental co-operation and co-ordination of facilities and programs already operating, rather than the establishment of another separate department, particularly when the Department of Defence Production is to handle these functions? May I call it five o'clock, Mr. Chairman?

ARTS, LETTERS AND SCIENCES CANADIAN UNIVERSITY SERVICE OVERSEAS   REQUEST FOR FINANCIAL SUPPORT
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the desirability of
University Service Overseas
supporting financially the Canadian university service overseas which helps young Canadians to go abroad to share their skills, training and humanity in those countries where such help is needed.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I was assisted, in phrasing my motion, although I must admit perhaps unknown to the person involved, by the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald). I phrased the motion in a manner which I felt would be acceptable to the government. The proposal is that the government consider, if it is desirable, giving financial support to the Canadian university service overseas. As is sometimes the habit in our neighbouring country to the south, perhaps more imaginative names are used in connection with projects of this sort. Of course, the name that has been used in the United States is "peace corps". The scheme in that country is much more government oriented, if I may use that phrase, than this motion would propose.
I have no exaggerated or grandiose sums of money in mind. I do suggest that $100,000 spent by the government in helping university students serve in other countries would be returned, if money must be returned, manyfold in good will and better understanding. I think, as is the case in so many instances with governments, such assistance would be helpful to the wider development of the giver as well as those receiving the benefit. It seems that with government today we must exercise some judgment as to priorities. I am a believer in priority. It seems to me that CUSO is an example of a service which is entitled to a priority, if any are, in so far as government financial assistance is concerned.
Perhaps we would have to say that $100,000 is an infinitesimal amount in relation to actual federal spending. I believe the house is entitled to an explanation of CUSO and what it is attempting to do. I can do no better than to quote from this information bulletin. It is interesting to note that CUSO was formed on June 6, 1961. The full title is Canadian university service overseas. It was established as a national co-ordinating agency to develop and promote schemes for sending Canadians to serve overseas. The initiative for the establishment of this body came from Canadian universities and several national organizations. CUSO works closely with national and local organizations in Canada and provides liaison with government international organizations and other agencies abroad.
Its functions have been defined in the following terms:
(a)	To initiate and operate, either alone or in co-operation with other organizations, schemes that will enable suitably qualified graduates, normally

University Service Overseas resident in Canada, to serve in countries overseas that have indicated their readiness to receive such persons;
(b)	To solicit and administer funds to cover the costs both of such schemes and of any activities ancillary thereto;
(c)	To assist, in such ways as the service may from time to time determine, other agencies which may be engaged in schemes of a similar nature.
CUSO is a means of providing opportunities for Canadians to serve abroad in conditions similar to those under which persons in the host countries also serve their fellow citizens. The organization hopes the scheme will promote greater understanding among the participants and serve as a gesture of international good will and co-operation. Graduates will only be sent abroad in response to specific requests for their services by governments and other appropriate agencies. They will not go as experts but as junior personnel who serve on a basis of equality with those with whom they live and work.
The need for funds is underlined by the fact that this year there are only sufficient funds available to send a fraction of the volunteers. I feel that this speaks well for Canadians in universities. As we have come to expect from young Canadians, the number of volunteers is far greater than the funds available to send them abroad.
A motion somewhat similar to the one being considered today was debated in this house on December 10. I think it is interesting to reread the debate. The proposal then was that the government establish a Canadian youth service, a government-sponsored scheme, to enable young Canadians to go abroad. I was struck by an observation of the hon. member for Rosedale during that debate. He properly pointed out that rather than duplicate existing services, his specific, and he said specific, recommendation was that the federal government give assistance to the CUSO program by way of grants. I reread his words over the week end and I take some comfort from them. If I can interpret his words, and perhaps this is dangerous, I assume he meant that the government should look favourably upon assisting CUSO, an established organization. The hon. member who made this very sensible recommendation is now parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice and, of course, is in a position to influence the government to accept this recommendation. This makes me much more hopeful that the motion will have widespread approval from members on all sides of the house.
The government, after all, is in no way committed by accepting the motion, because the motion merely requests that consideration be given to the desirability of granting

financial support. Rather than have the hon. member quote himself, which is a habit all too prevalent in parliaments in this and other countries, I should like the privilege of quoting him. I refer to Hansard for December 10, 1962, page 2506, where I find these words:
While I support the general principle of the resolution my specific recommendation would be that the federal government should give assistance to this program by way of grants to existing organizations. Second, I think the federal government to the greatest degree within its power should through its own facilities publicize both the availability of these services and the nature of the work that is done. The qualification which I would have regarding creating an independent government authority to administer this program is that I feel the universities should continue to be autonomous within this field and should administer the program.
If I could interpolate here, I would say I could not agree with the hon. member more.
The university faculties and students are in a better position to judge the applicants coming forward, and what is more, by having it in the hands of the universities you take away any suggestion of government interference and control which in this country might tend to discourage private contribution to the fund,-
By the way, Mr. Speaker, private contributions to the fund are being solicited at present and I believe those contributions, plus a generous government grant, would make it possible for this large number of Canadian university students to proceed overseas.
I have restrained myself from making a very lengthy speech because I hope the motion will receive general approval and that we can go on to other things. I sincerely ask the support of all hon. members of the house for it.
