speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to present the views held by the New Democratic party with regard to this resolution and the desirability of supporting financially the Canadian university service overseas. I suggest it is important we give thought to the image that is created

by Canadians wherever they go outside Canada. No matter where they went in two world wars our men gave a very fine impression of Canada, which even today is reflected in many of the agencies of the United Nations.
Mr. Speaker, if you were to go to New York and mingle with the representatives of the United Nations you would be very proud of the record of Canada in all international areas. Likewise, if you were to go to the International Labour Organization in Geneva and to the UNESCO organization in Paris you would get the same impression that, generally speaking, people throughout the world think well of Canada. One reason for this is that people do not think of us as an aggressive nation but as a nation prepared, within the limits of its capabilities, to offer assistance in one way or another to people in need.
At the present time there are many teachers in Europe serving the families of our men overseas and giving a good impression wherever they go. Here in Canada we know the great benefits which come from the commonwealth exchange of teachers and students. Several thousand commonwealth students are scattered across our country, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, attending Canadian universities. They benefit from life in Canada, but so also do we. I have had occasion to associate to some extent with overseas university students here in Canada, and it is a stimulating experience to meet them and discuss their problems from their points of view.
I suggest we should give our support to this motion as a peace project because the promotion of peace falls into various categories. We mostly think of defence arrangements, but that is only one way in which we can work for peace. Another way is to keep our own house in order so that when people think of Canada they think of a strong nation which gives fair treatment to everybody. Another way we can work for peace is by doing the very thing which the Canadian university service overseas organization is prepared to do, to provide a variety of services to people who are in need.
I am very happy to say, Mr. Speaker, that the New Democratic party urges support of this motion as a practical contribution to peace throughout the world.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it hardly seems necessary for me to stand up and support this motion as all hon. members who have spoken so far have supported it. However I would like to add my little contribution and perhaps a few more details might be helpful to some hon. members who are not familiar with the scheme.
In the first instance its purpose is to help those countries, which we would consider not so developed as ours, to have the assistance of people who are experts in certain lines. In the main these are teachers. Out of the 78 persons who have been sent to give this assistance during the last two years some 62 were teachers. These people only go to countries who ask for their help. They do not go unless definite requests are received for their services, and they live on the same salary levels and under the same living conditions as the people they are helping. This is particularly worthy of note because, in doing so, they do what the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Webster) suggested, namely they convince these people they are anxious to help them and give all the types of assistance we can possibly provide.
They go as junior experts, if we might call them that, and Canada is uniquely qualified to provide these services. Our historical background is one of the reasons why we are so qualified. We have a colonial background and most of the countries to which our people go realize this, so they feel kinship towards

University Service Overseas our junior experts. Then, too, we are fortunate in having two main races in Canada, and a great many French speaking people are required. In fact a substantial proportion of the people who go abroad to give these services are French speaking Canadians. I think too, that because we are the kind of country we are, our people who provide these services can do so in a proper spirit of humility. I think they lack the extreme nationalistic viewpoint which is noticeable in the nationals of some great nations, and consequently I think they are better received.
Last night at 10.30 the C.B.C. presented an excellent program showing the progress that has been made in many of these countries- countries such as India, Indonesia, the country of the Incas, and so on. It showed the progress that is being made in these countries in conquering man's main enemy, hunger. These people suffer not only from having too large a population, but also from a great ignorance of just how to attack their problem. It was evident in that program that this was the real attack being made, an attempt to instruct them in order that they could conquer their own difficulties. I think hon. members will agree with me that this is the proper way in which to attack the problem, by a program of self-help; in other words, show them how and let them work out their own solution. This the program certainly made evident.
This is what CUSO is trying to do. It is trying to send people out who will help to bring an end to this ignorance. It is trying to bring the benefits of education to those who need it far more than we do. Some other organizations also realize this need. In particular I would mention the Canadian Teachers' Federation, which is doing what it can along the same line. It expects to send some 12 to 15 teachers away this year to do exactly the same thing CUSO is doing. President Kennedy said recently that the real division in the world today was not between east and west but was primarily between the rich and the poor. Very probably what he had in mind was that even if the so-called cold war was brought to an end, we would still be faced with world conflict between the "haves" and the "have nots". It is very encouraging to see that we are perhaps a little closer to a solution of the cold war because of the news we heard this morning, that President Kennedy, Mr. Khrushchev and Mr. Macmillan are to meet soon.
We have all heard the argument that three quarters of the world's population go to bed hungry every night. If we can, by a small grant-I think the suggested sum of $100,000 is certainly a small grant for a country such as ours-in some small measure convince these


people that we are willing to do our part to' help them conquer this great handicap of hunger, it will bear very, very good fruit int the future. Also, an intelligent view of this question should convince us that there is an imperative need for Canada to develop the closest and friendliest relations with each of these countries. Our students will certainly do this for us while they are in these other countries, and on their return I am quite convinced they will have a very great levelling effect on the mass of public opinion in Canada,, which I think is a very desirable thing. Canadians generally are a sympathetic and considerate people and I am sure they will want their government to give what assistance it can to countries which in this way are asking, for our assistance.
Miss Pauline Jewel! (Northumberland): Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member whose motion this is and the speakers who have preceded me, I too am in favour of and sympathetic to CUSO. As the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Cantelon) said, this organization brings to its work a very marked degree of humility, having anything but the sort of "do good" attitude that so many of us deplore in so many so-called charitable activities. The young people involved in CUSO, as the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Fairweather) noted, go out as junior personnel and serve on a basis of equality with those with whom they will live and work. They are not necessarily full-blown experts; they are young university graduates. I think the average age of the group now in the field is about 24. They have not a great deal of expertise, but they have the one thing that matters most, a great desire to serve, a great desire to do something helpful and useful in the world either at home or abroad. They are particularly concerned with going abroad because, as we all well know, it is in the so-called "have not" or less developed nations of the world that help is particularly needed. Most of them, I understand, went as teachers in 1961 and 1962, although there have also been nurses and doctors, as well as people without any formal training at all. They live in the communities to which they go under conditions on a par with those of the people there, and I understand that they go alone to these communities. Unlike the United States peace corps, where they go in pairs, under CUSO the young people go alone into the communities and in this way become even more intimately and closely involved. It is therefore an organization which I should think it would be almost impossible for anyone in this house, or indeed anywhere, not to look upon very favourably and with understanding.
The difficulty with which CUSO is faced, as the hon. member for Royal pointed out, is a financial one. Unfortunately this is a difficulty

laced by the government of Canada as well. CUSO is now undertaking, I believe, a drive for funds of around $185,000. This drive has been going on since about February or March of this year, and to date I believe they have got about $90,000 to $100,000. This has been entirely from private sources. As was pointed out, our peace corps, our CUSO, is quite different from the United States peace corps in that it is a private, not a government, organization. It is privately financed and organized. The hope is to attain the objective of $185,000. To the best of my knowledge CUSO itself has not asked for government assistance to help it attain this figure. I understand from them and from the Canadian universities federation, under whose administrative wing CUSO operates, that they may well in a few months' time be approaching the government for financial help. From my conversations with the persons involved in CUSO-and of course I have had many in the past, having been as you know, Mr. Speaker, on a university staff-my understanding is that they would like, if possible, to derive their funds from private sources. If, however, it becomes absolutely out of the question to raise the needed funds in this way, I have no doubt that they will be coming to the government and in particular to the minister of external affairs (Mr. Martin), for help.
I should like to say here that the minister of external affairs has at his side someone who might be even more influential in securing help for CUSO than the hon. member for Royal or, if I may so, even the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Macdonald) -

-or myself. I am referring to Duncan Edmonds, who was a former colleague of mine at Carleton University and is now special assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin). Mr. Edmonds has been very active in CUSO activities. I do not know that he is a graduate of CUSO, but I know that last summer he was a graduate of Crossroads Africa. He is extremely enthusiastic and I know he will do his best when the time comes for us, as I am sure it will, to put a strong case forward on this matter. I am sure the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) is himself well aware of the problem, and, even though he has not been formally asked to do so, has already considered the kind of straits CUSO may get into if, for one reason or another, the campaign is not successful, say, by September.
For all I think very highly of CUSO, as, I am sure, do other hon. members here, it is important for us to keep in mind a great
University Service Overseas many other volunteer agencies and private societies which work in the external aid field. I was amazed to discover how many there are and the variety of tasks they undertake. There are, of course, the church groups of all denominations which have, I suppose, been in the field the longest. There are private societies which collect books, clothing and medicine for shipment to Asia and Africa, paying all expenses, including transportation. The Canadian Teachers' Federation will send abroad this year between 18 and 20 secondary schoolteachers, all costs being met out of funds collected by Canadian teachers in the various provinces. The alliance of hospital auxiliaries has been operating on funds contributed across Canada, and this organization has been supplying medical equipment to the developing nations. It also offers some modest scholarships in Canada, and ships overseas thousands of copies of its publications. Then there is the African students foundation which is one of my own favourites. The foundation has close to 100 students studying in Canadian universities'-students from Africa brought to Canada to study with the help of funds raised entirely by this organization. Carrying on similar work is Les Amites Quebec-Afrique.
In all, there are between 70 and 90 organizations engaged in the external aid field in some way or other, and to the best of my knowledge the only ones which now get aid from the Canadian government are the Canadian Red Cross Society and the United Nations Association. It therefore will, undoubtedly, become a matter of some importance to the government whether it should select CUSO, specifically, as an organization to be helped or whether consideration should be given on a broader scale to the needs of other organizations such as, for example, the African students foundation.
I think this question will come to the attention of the government more forcefully this year than ever before because of a new development which is taking place. To be more precise, it is taking place next Monday, June 17, I think, in Ottawa-a meeting of representatives of all these private societies and organizations, including CUSO. This will be the first meeting of what is called the national committee on Canada's participation in social development abroad. It is being held under the auspices of the overseas institute of Canada and its purpose is to find out what agencies there are in the field of external aid, what they are doing, what they feel should be done, and what kind of help they need. In addition, the committee will be considering how to raise funds, whether some ideas or assistance could be given in helping to raise funds and, generally, the most effective ways

University Service Overseas of tackling the problem of world wide distress, both by private agencies and by government. The government will, I am sure, send an observer to this meeting. Perhaps someone from the external aid office will be giving a paper. Certainly, a representative will be involved as an observer.
This raises the question as to where Canadian government or public funds should go in the field of external aid. Just as CUSO has difficulty in raising funds, so the government has a problem here as well. I do not know, but I would guess that the government is probably giving first priority to restoring the full amount of the Colombo plan expenditure which, as hon. members may know, was running at $50 million a year and which was cut last year to $41.5 million. It seems to me there is a great deal to be said for restoring this grant as soon as possible. Indeed, there is much to be said for increasing the amount. I would like to see it doubled. Then the government already has in operation a number of other aid programs in addition to the Colombo plan. First, there is the program of assistance to the West Indies. This is a $10 million program. Second, there is participation in the commonwealth educational program under which we provide approximately 250 scholarships at an annual cost of $1 million. This is a program in which all the less developed members of the commonwealth share. Third, there is our program of assistance to the commonwealth countries of Africa, amounting to about $3.5 million a year. Fourth, there are smaller programs of assistance, shortly to be amalgamated, for the benefit of British Guiana, British Honduras and Hong Kong. Fifth, there is the program of educational assistance to the French states of Africa.
These are five continuing programs which have all proved their worth, and from what I have been able to discover they should all be encouraged. Indeed, perhaps additions should be made to them. The demands on the government in the field of external aid in the direction of restoring the cutback in the Colombo plan expenditure, as a first step to increasing it if possible, besides doing something more in the programs in which it is already involved, make it unlikely that at this particular moment it will begin to give aid to agencies which up to now have been providing their own funds. This is not to say it will not consider doing so in the future if the agencies concerned really cannot make a go of it.
I am sure the government will give this matter sympathetic consideration, and I am sure all of us who are interested will do our best to see it does so, not by means of a


formal motion in this house but, I would hope, by all of us who are interested in these matters getting together and descending on the government.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity of speaking for a few minutes in support of this motion. I believe that if ever there was a motion which should enjoy the support of every hon. member in this house, it is the one now before us. The reason I desire to speak for a few moments is because I have had the opportunity of seeing these young men, under the plan in operation, in Africa. I might say that it makes one absolutely proud to see the work they are doing and the admiration in which they are held by the people in the countries in which they work.
Six hon. members from this House of Commons had the opportunity last fall of spending six or seven weeks in Nigeria, and we travelled the entire country. Wherever we went we had the opportunity of meeting some of these young people who are working under this plan, and sharing their abilities, skills and humanities in countries and amongst people where such are needed. Wherever we went, whether we met these people in a village or a city, we were told at all times how happy the people were with these young people, and were asked if we could not send them some more. They definitely needed more of the type of assistance that these Canadians have been giving and are giving. I think that request can most certainly be understood if

I just use as an example the country we travelled in last year. Here we have a country which is a member of the commonwealth. It has 42 million people, and for those 42 million people there are 81 doctors and 33 dentists. The only places you see hospitals are in the major cities, and in some of them there is only one doctor. At every hospital there is a line-up of between 500 to 1,000 outpatients every morning, most of whom, of course, have to be turned away. It is a country where one child out of two dies at birth. These countries in Africa are countries with problems, and these young people under this plan are trying to offer a contribution on behalf of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I felt I just had to get up and say how proud I myself was in travelling around Africa last year and seeing what these 24 people, I think it is, are doing in one country. But a lot more are needed and we have the responsibility, in assisting this university plan, of seeing that if the money required cannot be obtained from private sources this government should certainly consider the advisability of giving official aid through the medium of the university for what I maintain is a wonderful and worthwhile plan for those in need, a plan contributed to by our country of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, education is the concern of all conscientious citizens, and all those responsible for the progress made in that field deserve great praise.
In Canada, primary and secondary education is given under improved conditions both for the pupils and the teachers.
University education is being dispensed to an increasing number of students. Technical education has progressed throughout the country. We were happy to hear today, from the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen), that the federal government will continue to offer its program of assistance to the provinces for the building of technical schools.
Mr. Speaker, Canada is providing generously for the education of her children. Realizing how advantageous education could be, university teachers and students have joined together to promote the future of education in less fortunate countries. The voice of those underdeveloped countries was heard at the United Nations and in other international forums. Such appeals have been supported by people from all corners of the globe, and were echoed in a most fraternal way by Pope John XXIII who will be remembered as the apostle of brotherhood.
University Service Overseas
In Canada, that generous idea come to life on June 6, 1961. On that occasion, representatives of 21 Canadian universities and 22 corporations laid the groundwork for Canadian university services overseas, known as CUSO.
This came in addition to the aid Canada was already giving to the underdeveloped countries, because we know that within the United Nations in 1961 Canada as a member of that organization, subscribed a total amount of $7,440,000 to international aid and assistance funds to underdeveloped countries.
It is in a spirit of generosity that our Canadian universities got together to set up this Canadian university service overseas. Seventy eight Canadian graduates were members of the 1961-62 group. In the light of the first year's experience, 120 graduates will be members of the 1962-63 group.
The organization known as the foundation of Canadian universities is an example of national achievement due to the co-operation of our two official ethnical groups which have contributed to promote this project by recruiting and selecting people from all Canadian universities.
Out of a total of 78 students, Laval University and the University of Montreal contributed 20 French speaking candidates, and it is estimated that 40 French speaking candidates will be among the next group of 120 graduates.
This fact is worthy of being mentioned; it is an example to all the organizations of the federal civil service and to the crown corporations that if we really want to recruit and select people in conformity with our aspirations, the candidates are many and have the required qualifications to play their part in all fields of Canadian activity. The federal civil service and the crown corporations have but to imitate the Canadian university service overseas in its recruiting and selection methods, and they will thus be in a position to give a more equitable share to French speaking Canadians in the administration of the country.
Mr. Speaker, allow me to point out to the house that a great Canadian educator, Rev. Father Georges Henri Levesque, has left for Rouanda. After having set up the social science department at Laval University, in Quebec, Father Levesque leaves Canada to found a university in Africa. Pioneer in the field of education in Canada, Father Levesque

University Service Overseas wants to help a young country, anxious to make strides in education. Other Canadian educators, no doubt, will go over to assist Father Levesque in his task.
Mr. Speaker, I have also been told today that five professors from the Catholic school board of Montreal will give refresher courses this summer to some professors from Gabon. These are two examples of Canadian efforts towards very deserving programs of mutual assistance between nations.
The hon. member for Royal (Mr. Fair-weather) suggests direct financial assistance by the federal government to the Canadian university service overseas. I take leave to suggest a middle course to the proposal by the hon. member. Let us ask the Canadian Universities Foundation to make an annual grant to be added to subscriptions paid to the Canadian university service overseas by individuals, organizations and companies.
The Canadian university service overseas has an annual budget of $200,000 and has succeeded in collecting $100,000 in private donations. The Canadian Universities Foundation must keep its control and direction over the Canadian university service overseas, but the interference of the federal government by a direct contribution would in time wash out the characteristics which the founders had planned for this establishment.
The countries where our graduates are sent pay the salaries and, in a few cases only, the transportation costs. To date, in two years of operation, transportation is our major expense item.
Could the government not assist through its transportation services our graduates who must travel to far off lands? Have the R.C.A.F., the Department of Transport and the Department of External Affairs ever been consulted on that matter? Could not the Canada Council set up a scholarship system under the title of "post-university study and research"?
I am glad that once again, the Canadian university service overseas program was brought before the house and our discussion will make us ever more conscious of the part Canada must play the world over as an independent and prosperous nation helping other less developed nations who also have a right to independence and prosperity. Establishment of Industry Department AFTER RECESS
The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, at five o'clock I was just beginning my remarks on this important subject and pointing out how happy I was to see that even the Liberal party now recognizes that we have to move very vigorously in the area of industrial decentralization, industrial diversification and industrial development. During the critical years when Canada was faced with profound changes not only internally but also externally, the attitude towards this problem of assisting our economy in the change from primary production to secondary production was largely left to the laissez faire process. I made some reference to the historical past in this respect which resulted in a great economic upsurge following world war II and which was largely brought about by external factors. The problem of internal Canadian adaptation to the modern world was worsened rather than lessened in that industry failed to diversify. It remained geared to the demands of defence requirements and also was largely concentrated in the two central provinces. This, of course, only intensified the problems that have dogged confederation ever since 1867, namely the concentration of population in a small area of Canada, the concentration of financial interests and so forth. This problem, aggravated by the failure to act vigorously during the years 1945 into the mid 50's, has created some of the more serious difficulties within our system of confederation at the present time.
I was interested to note that the Department of Defence Production is the chosen instrument to take over the functions. I expressed some surprise because the record of the defence production department in the past has not been salutary so far as resolving these basic difficulties in Canada's body politic to which I have referred. This leads me to comment further on the tendency in Canada for industrial development to take the lines of least resistance and concentrate in the areas of defence requirements. I think the unhappy experience of Avro is the classical example in this regard. Here was a company that put all its eggs in one basket in terms of industrial development with the rather disastrous consequences which occurred in the changing circumstances of the mid 50's. The tragedy of the Avro aircraft is very closely associated with this laissez faire attitude of the former Liberal administration towards industrial development. I recall the debates in this house when the Avro jetliner project was scrapped in favour of a military program which it was felt at that time was necessitated

Establishment of Industry Department by the outbreak of the Korean war. I kept some of the items relating to this subject because of my interest in the matter, coming as I do from an area of Canada which felt keenly the need for industrial development and stimulation.
I kept an item from the issue of the Avro Canada Magazine back in March 1950 concerning the jetliner which points out, and I quote:
As you know, the jetliner will soon complete its pressurization tests in the air and then go on to obtain its American certificate of airworthiness. After that, we will try to sell it throughout the world because there seem to be no technical or aerodynamic snags to upset us. We hope to start by selling the jetliner right here in Canada and the United States operators have shown a definite interest in it. The jetliner is being flown to England this summer with the view of interesting British and European operators. There is considerable interest in this aircraft in Australia and there might also be some in South America. We are hoping that the second jetliner will soon be ready to help us out in our sales tours and demonstrations.
Now, unfortunately, shortly after that statement was made the whole project was cancelled and the industry returned to its defence orientation. I felt at the time, and many others were of a similar opinion, that Canada had lost a great industrial opportunity because this jetliner had flown simultaneously with the de Havilland Comet. If the project had been carried forward, if there had been careful planning and careful co-ordination within government departments, we would have had a balanced aircraft industry in that important industrial area of Toronto rather than the lopsided development which resulted in the Avro economic difficulties of the mid 50's.
Then, another example of this failure to give any direction or even co-ordination during those critical years when all parts of Canada were crying for guidance from the former Liberal government, was the T.C.A. episode in the city of Winnipeg. Winnipeg had been chosen as the T.C.A. repair centre. I just happen to have a clipping from the Winnipeg Free Press of Thursday, June 6 which outlines in a clear-cut way how the present problems of T.C.A. in the city of Winnipeg began. The Free Press article is headed, "A History of Deception". In order to outline what the editors of that newspaper mean by that I am going to give one or two quotations from the editorial.
In 1948 Mr. C. D. Howe, then minister of trade, said in reply to queries that T.C.A. had no intention of moving its main department from Winnipeg. He said that some operating department heads might move, but that 95 per cent of the company's activities would remain centred in Winnipeg.
This sounded like a very sensible program, in view of the geographic circumstances in

Canada and also in view of the need to decentralize industrial activities. We know what happened shortly after that, and the Free Press article gives in some detail the sorry pattern of withdrawal from that basic position over the years until, at the present time, the citizens of Winnipeg and particularly the employees of T.C.A. are not even certain that the telegram that was sent during the course of the last election campaign meant what it said. The telegram, in effect, said that the proper location of T.C.A. facilities and services would be determined in a manner which would be fair and equitable to the city of Winnipeg. This is almost a paraphrase of the original statement which was made in 1948 by the then minister of trade and commerce.
Now, Mr. Chairman, this indicates that at the time there was a real need for a program that would co-ordinate and encourage industrial decentralization and diversification. There was no action forthcoming from the then Liberal government. The provinces took the matter into their own hands and, almost without exception, each of the provincial governments have established very strong and virile industrial development programs.
Just to illustrate this point I could point out the progress that has been made in the province of Manitoba where for the past four years, ever since Hon. Mr. Roblin became premier, they have moved forward with a very vigorous program of industrial development. They have divided the province into regional areas to avoid the difficulty of internecine strife between small local municipalities. They conceive of industrial potential in terms of regions rather than local municipalities. Recently the business community, the manufacturing community, the voluntary groups associated with these sectors of the economy, working in close co-operation with the provincial government have produced an excellent report on the economic prospects of that province which will be implemented over the next few years.
This is typical of the programs that have been carried out in each of the provinces. They had to undertake this work and move into this area because of the inactivity of the former Liberal administration. This, Mr. Chairman, indicates that two things must take place. We are faced with the proposal that everything which has been going forward in the provinces, as well as in the various departments of government, at the federal level is now going to be concentrated in a new department of industry. The preliminary statement of the Prime Minister would suggest that the Department of Defence Production is going to be the chosen instrument in this regard, and I would like to

emphasize that there is a strong possibility, if the pattern of the Liberal government when it was formerly in power is resumed, for these matters once again to be considered in isolation.
I would like to emphasize just as strongly as I can that you cannot carry out this important task of encouraging the development of secondary industries, of assisting Canada in moving as rapidly as possible from primary production to secondary production, unless you take into consideration the intragovernmental aspects, that is to say, cooperation between the various departments of government that are involved in this process.
I want to congratulate the Minister of Labour on his statement this afternoon to the effect that programs will be undertaken, or I should say continued, to stimulate employment. In his statement he emphasized the necessity for the closest possible coordination and co-operation between the various departments of government. In so doing he endorsed the policy carried out by the former Conservative administration. The programs he outlined are programs that are already under way or were in contemplation. The only differences were slight modifications for the sake of effect. Our administration realized that government today can only be carried on successfully if ministers and departments work together for the betterment of the whole. This is demonstrated in the work of the national energy board which dealt very successfully in that field of activity. Again today the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources is taking one further step in the development of the national resources ministers council, which has been in process of formation for the past two years. I cannot overemphasize the necessity of intra-governmental co-operation as well as inter-governmental co-operation.
To bring my remarks to a conclusion there is just one other aspect I wish to mention. The Glassco report had some words to say on these matters, and it is to be noted that it made some strong recommendations concerning the functions of the Department of Defence Production. I trust that in its desire to introduce a half-baked program which was drawn out of the blue during an election campaign to support a slogan with similar dubious origins, the slogan of 60 days of action, the government will not be stampeded into completely ignoring the very significant recommendations of the Glassco report. It seems to me that if the department is to achieve this aim it may find it will have to encourage certain amalgamations of Canadian industry-if you like, a certain rationalization of some of our manufacturing industries-so they can produce at low cost and compete in world markets. I suggest that our present anti-combines legislation is too weak to protect effectively the consumers and small business from the price-fixing activities of certain large business combines-and I expect we shall have more of this kind of activity in the future.
The anti-combines laws of this country were recently studied by two university professors G. Rosenbluth and H. G. Thorburn. They published their findings in a book called Canadian Anti-Combines Administration 19521960. The central argument of these authors is that Canadian combines legislation is based on a mistaken concept-the "cops and robbers" concept. According to this viewpoint, monopolistic or anti-competitive practices are the infrequent acts of a criminal minority who represent exceptions to a generally competitive and law-abiding business community. It follows from this assumption that the role of the combines machinery is to seek out these deviates and bring them to justice before the courts.
The authors believe that these very limited terms of reference prevent a solution of the real problem. They point out that monopolistic practices are not an aberration from the norm but, rather, are widespread and constitute the typical business environment. They favour the view that the preservation of competition requires constant attention by the government in order to render the economic environment competitive and to reduce the attractiveness of monopolistic arrangements. In shaping the economic environment all the

During 1962 Canada's gross national product-that is, the sum total of all goods and services produced in Canada during the year-increased by 8 per cent. The increase in our national production-that is, the gross national product less the increase in prices which took place during the year, which is therefore the true measure of the increase in national output-was 7 per cent. With regard to this matter, Mr. Chairman, I think that the government should consider the unemployment problem under a quite different angle than the industrial one. And as far as the field of labour is concerned, Mr. Chairman, I would submit the following thesis to the Prime Minister. It has been recognized that the labour and employment field comprises three sections.
First of all, there is what we may call the production section. Now, 100 or 150 years ago, the whole population applied itself to production. The shoemaker made the shoes himself which he put in his showcase and sold them himself. The use of machinery also was part of productive labour, because automation had not yet been discovered. Indeed, today some industries may produce quantities of goods with only very few men, and at this point the second section appears in the field of labour, that is the marketing section. There are some men who are employed in production and others in marketing and sales. The latter created a new source of employment, but today, we have come to the point where industry grabs all the labour it can.
On the other hand, there is an excess of labour in the marketing field. Indeed, salesmen can even be seen going from door to door offering shoe laces, dictionaries, bibles, perfume, and what have you. Now, as the marketing and sales field is already overcrowded, the unemployment problem will scarcely be solved that way, nor even by trying to employ all Canadians in industry.

Mr. Chairman, I also note that speaking about industrial protection, the Prime Minister said it was not by maintaining high tariffs that we would sell our goods.
Well, let us not forget that products made in Canada are more expensive than goods made in other countries and that when tariff barriers are removed, less expensive products will sell first. In fact, why are our products more expensive than those made in the United States? Because our taxes are higher. Indeed, it costs no more to make a package of cigarettes in the United States than in Canada, because it is the same tobacco and the same paper. Nevertheless, Americans pay 27 or 28 cents, while Canadians have to pay 40 cents. The difference in the price goes in taxes.
If the department of industry is expected to launch into a reduction of tariff barriers, I agree, because I am in favour of trade between nations, but to begin with, we must stabilize our prices in order to compete with other countries in imports and exports. And to do that, we will have first to reduce the taxes on our products.
Mr. Chairman, those were the few observations I wished to make. In fact, I have another one, following some observations by the right hon. Prime Minister who said, speaking about an area development agency:
The areas which concern us are those where unemployment is prevailing-
Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the Prime Minister to name just one region in Canada where unemployment is not prevailing, only one. In fact, even in his riding unemployment is rife.

Now, if he is concerned about the regions where unemployment is prevailing, he must realize that unemployment exists all across the country because it is not a localized matter due to geographic or transportation circumstances. Unemployment is a national plague, all across the country. It ignores regional frontiers and extends to all areas, in every corner of the country and it will have to be eradicated everywhere.
Mr. Chairman, the Prime Minister also stated:
-the government is by no means blind to the difficulties and problems which will arise and which the new department, if it is set up, will have to face.
Mr. Chairman, it is not the department of industry which will settle the problems everywhere. I do not see why new problems should arise, provided the new department guides the economy in the right direction; if such is not the case, not only will it fail to solve the problems, but it will not do anything constructive.
Without wishing to criticize in any way the measure put forward by the Prime Minister, I felt I had to call his attention to a few problems that will come up. I felt I had to tell him also that even if he sets up a department such as the department of industry, even if he manages to achieve the purposes of paragraphs (a), (b) and (c), that is if he appoints a minister and deputy minister, if he sets up a Canadian development corporation and if he raises the salaries of the minister and the deputy minister, that will not help him solve the problems he seemed to mention in the speech he made last Friday. Let him rather think of developing other fields of human activities that will open new opportunities, because those we have now, that is factory work or merchandising, are already saturated.
It might be possible to establish new industries or at least to help the Canadian people, for example, in industries such as steel, asbestos and many others.
It is recognized that our building industry is greatly developed, but why is it not developed even more, especially when there is such a need for slum clearance, when there is a need for more than 800,000 new homes in Canada. There is an industry where assistance is badly needed and it should not be given by trying to teach the plumber how to install his pipes or the contractor how to
10, 1963	873
Establishment of Industry Department build a house, but first and, foremost, by enabling the ordinary Canadian citizen to go and buy himself a house. Let us leave the house builder alone. He will manage to build the house. Let us reduce taxes, and the house will cost less. Let us reduce interest rates of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and the ordinary Canadian will be able to buy his house, and you will see how many plumbers, electricians and workers are able to buy a decent house and that Canada is able to provide a home for each and every Canadian citizen.
If the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), the ministers, all members can live in proper houses, it means that, at the time, we had the manpower, the skills, and the materials necessary to build them. Well, Mr. Chairman, I say to the Prime Minister that we have everything we need in Canada to build houses for all Canadians. The solution is to help the humble folks to buy their houses. That is the problem.
It is simple, nobody need have invented gunpowder to be able to discover that.
So, I believe that the first concern of this department of industry should be to help Canadians to buy what industry can produce. If the department of industry can do that, Mr. Chairman, the day Canada will be able to buy what its industry can produce, it will be possible to say of the present Prime Minister that he has introduced the best measure ever carried by a government here, in Ottawa, an act which will have settled the problem that faces Canadians in allowing them to buy, to acquire all the wealth human industry and primary resources can give.

Mr. Chairman, I would not like to see the setting up of this new department becoming an opportunity for the present government to interfere with provincial jurisdiction in industrial and economic matters.
We are very anxious to know whether the government has contacted the ministers or the premiers of each province to see if provinces such as Quebec and Ontario, as well as others, are in favour of the establishment, by the federal government, of a department of industry, so that the jurisdiction of each province in this field shall be respected.
Indeed the new minister who will be appointed to head this department, should give us information on this point. However, the fact that the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Drury) will head this department is a
874	HOUSE OF
Establishment of Industry Department somewhat comforting thought. If the minister responsible for this department had been the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean (Mr. Lamontagne), we should have been quite worried about the autonomy of the provinces, for the hon. member is a known advocate of centralization and, in the past, he has disregarded the rights of the provinces.
In any case, we are anxious to learn whether the Prime Minister has consulted with the premiers and sought their co-operation and whether the provinces were willing to co-operate. As far as the province of Quebec is concerned, we know of the many ultimatums which the Lesage government has served on the federal government.
Mr. Chairman, it would be unfortunate if this new department were to become an opportunity for intrusion into provincial jurisdiction, delayed the development of confederation and rather jeopardized it.
Mr. Chairman, the resolution specifies that the minister shall have certain experts to advise him.
I strongly suggest that he recruit the majority of these experts in the provinces where there is less heavy industries, such as the province of Quebec and the maritime provinces. We all know that these provinces suffer from a lack of heavy industry.
There is at present a national lack of balance which even affects national unity, for when there is an economic recession in some parts of the country, national unity is automatically affected and even the wealthier provinces are adversely affected.
It would also be advisable that the new minister, after having consulted with the provinces so as to avoid encroachment in their respective jurisdictions, find ways and means of processing our raw materials domestically.
Today, we see carloads of nickel ingots, carloads of iron ore being shipped direct to the United States where they are processed and manufactured, and then sold back to Canada.
If these raw materials were processed in Canada, our workers would thereby obtain jobs and additional income, and this would also bring extra taxes to our country.
We could also sell more abroad and get in this way more foreign currency which would contribute to decrease our trade deficit.
Everyone knows that the province of Quebec holds a record as far as the number of the unemployed is concerned. Forty per cent of the unemployed are from the province of


Quebec. Thus I ask the new minister to undertake a very special study in that field in order to give a lift to the economy of the province if possible, to bring in heavy industry, so that it can prosper like the other provinces-and this applies also to the mari-times, so that those provinces can increase their economic strength.
A few days ago a prominent professor at Queen's University during a lecture, stated this-and here I quote La Presse, the Friday edition, last June 7:
Quebec will need twenty years before it can hold an important place in industry.
Which means, Mr. Chairman, that the new head of that department has a long way to go and that he must work continuously to that end. I know that he has had vast experience, but I have to reproach him slightly, although I know that he is not the only one to blame. During the last world war, the Department of Defence Production established hardly any heavy defence industry in the maritimes and in the province of Quebec.
For example we find, in the county of Joli-ette-L'Assomption-Montcalm a branch of Canadian Arsenals which is called the Cherrier plant. That plant had an employment capacity of 15,000 men during the last war, and after the war that figure fell to 500 or 600 employees, where it remains now.
I ask the minister to work with all his might and to follow in his predecessor's footsteps, those of the former member for Lot-biniere, who secured from the Americans very important contracts to provide jobs for our workers, especially in the field of defence production.
I also advise the new minister to set up a Canadian textile council. Unfortunately, the former Liberal government neglected too long in the past the textile industry that is largely concentrated in eastern Ontario, Quebec and the maritimes
The textile industry has been described as ideal for Canada:
1.	Over 50 per cent of that industry is in Canadian hands;
2.	It employs the greatest number of workers during the winter, which reduces seasonal unemployment;
3.	It meets basic needs;
4.	It can be located in underdeveloped areas;
5.	It uses Canadian materials.
The primary and secondary textile industry is owned and operated by Canadians in

the proportion of 84 per cent, as against 48 per cent of Canadian industry in general. The labour force is at its highest from September to April and falls off during the summer months. That industry meets an obvious need of primary importance.
When a production need is felt, that industry can settle in areas where industry is totally non-existent, or almost, because of its great need for skilled and unskilled labour.
New industries have tried to locate in the maritime provinces but they had a great deal of difficulty because of the slowing down in production. There are numerous new synthetic Canadian products such as rayon, nylon, viscose and acetate.
Mr. Chairman, over 130 million pounds of refined pulp are used as raw material for the manufacture of rayon in the textile industry. The value of the pulp increases from 1 to 30 per cent per pound before use.
Almost 100 per cent of the Canadian wool production is used in our mills and most of our chemicals are of Canadian manufacture.
Please note, Mr. Chairman, that the textile industry alone employs the greatest number of workmen in Canada. It is more than the mining industry, 20 times more than all the petroleum industries, almost twice as much as the forest industry and almost twice as much as the paper industry.
I wanted to call the attention, Mr. Chairman, to the importance there is for this new department, in co-operation with the provinces, to promote and protect our textile industry. I know that the minister and the Prime Minister agree with me on that matter. The devaluation of the Canadian dollar greatly helped the textile industry during these last years. I wish I knew if the new minister agrees with me on that matter.
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to interfere with the provincial jurisdiction, but as a taxpayer and a citizen of a province, I also think it is reasonable that in the future, before granting a mining claim, the provinces concerned should set drastic conditions to foreign capital which will get them, so that in the long run, Canadians may become owners instead of always serving our powerful neighbours to the south.
We want to co-operate with the United States, but we also want them to give Cana-

Establishment of Industry Department dians a chance to participate in the executive boards. Need I have to remind you, Mr. Chairman, that foreign capitalists control 57 per cent of Canadian industries.
It is also a danger from a political point of view. We know something about it on this side of the house in view of certain events which took place recently. Following an electoral campaign, we know that foreign interests own more than 50 per cent of capital investments in this country and thus, could control our politics.
I would like foreign capital, which is always welcome in our country, to be placed under Canadian control. And as I said earlier, Americans should give Canadians an interest in American subsidiaries. It is also unfortunate to see Canadian industrialists who have succeeded through their efforts and in spite of competition, being forced to sell their business to foreign interests as soon as it is flourishing. The provinces should also restrict those transactions, but without interfering with the freedom of industries. There should be a special committee in every province to prevent Canadian industrialists who own a family concern from selling it to foreign interests. For instance, the Sorel Industries sold its forge to a large American steel mill. It is most unfortunate to see Canadians who have set up a successful business reach a point where they must sell it to foreign interests.
Mr. Chairman, I trust that the new department of industry will be cautious in all circumstances, especially concerning tariff matters, so that tariff rates will not be abolished. There is a refrigerator factory in my riding. If tariff rates were to be abolished, it would have to close down and lay off hundreds of workers.
The same thing could be said of agriculture. Customs tariffs should not be abolished. Our farm products especially should be protected against American dumping.
I also hope that the Canadian government will find new markets for our products so as to diversify our trade patterns. Our imports from the United States are larger than our exports, with the result that we have a trade deficit. The smallest change in the American protectionist policy has its effects in Canada.

In closing, I should like to express the wish that the new department of industry-will co-operate with the ministers of trade of the provinces for the establishment of the metric system in Canada. In the past, I had the opportunity of showing the great advantages that would ensue from the use of the metric system in conjunction with the imperial system of weights and measures. I have pointed out to the house the tremendous opportunities we have lost in the field of international trade, especially as far as precision tools and machinery are concerned. I should like to make the following constructive suggestion to the minister. In my opinion, a federal-provincial conference should be called if necessary, so that the metric system may be applied and taught in the schools.
The provinces should progressively adapt their highway traffic signs to the national standards to help our trade. Canada, the United States and a few other countries will soon be the only ones to recognize our present system.
Great Britain is said to be substituting the metric system for its system of weights and measures. In our country, if we want to be up to date and to compete on world markets, if we want to be leaders in world trade, we must go forward.
I hope the minister who is quite resourceful will consider these problems with the co-operation of the departments of trade and industry of the provinces, in order to leave no avenue unexplored in his efforts to check unemployment and increase our export trade.

Mr. Chairman, I have only a few remarks to make on this resolution to set up a department of industry. In view of the fact that the Prime Minister himself introduced this resolution and is obviously so interested in it, I think something should be said about areas like his own about which I presume he would find some difficulty in speaking owing to his position in this house. For many areas of Canada the area development agency is going to be the answer to a promise made by the Prime Minister and other members of the government to solve some of the industrial problems of areas similar to the one represented by the Prime Minister.
In combining these various agencies that the Prime Minister mentioned it would appear that for the second time in my experience

we are creating a new cabinet post and we hope that this has not been done to provide a job for a specific person but that a much broader application is involved. The former government established the Department of Forestry which has grown very rapidly but it is my personal feeling that maybe it was set up for a specific purpose and that it grew like Topsy after the original need was met.
I believe that area development can and will eventually be one of the major roles of government, and I am wondering, as did a previous speaker, whether this can be done by government that is pledged to the free enterprise system and to the maintenance of that system. I am wondering how you can say that you are going to have people brought into this new department to administer the department of industry and at the same time say that you are going to provide area development for those areas where industry is not now located.
I believe that in many parts of Canada industry location is going to be the most important question that the government will have to face. The Prime Minister's area, which has developed very rapidly, has reached a stage in less than 10 years that it took my area 50 years to reach. But the result has been the same. In both these areas we have had development. Social capital has been expanded beyond the needs of the people of the area at the present time. This has been done in many parts of Canada through basic industry development. Such development will still continue and will be encouraged in the normal way where industry can produce a product at a cost that makes it worth while to operate as in the case of the new mining development that is taking place in my area. Under normal circumstances these industries will develop themselves.
There are areas, however, where no new basic development is taking place and industry is going to have to be given a shot in the arm. Industry is going to have to be assisted and is actually going to have to be directed because if it did not need to be directed it would already have located in these areas.
It is quite true that many of the things that have been done in the last five years have been advantageous and have provided initiative to bring new industries into such areas. Yet if we look at most of the major areas of surplus manpower across Canada we will find that few industries have gone into those areas of their own volition. The cities, the

major consumption areas of the country, are still growing very rapidly while other areas are not growing at all.
The previous government, and I presume this government intends to do the same, gave financial assistance, direction and technical advice to induce industry to locate in specific areas that are known as disaster or distressed areas. This has resulted in many surprising things. I was interested to read in the Toronto Star not long ago that Nova Scotia now has a new rug manufacturing industry. If this industry had not been given some assistance by the maritime council, which has been helpful in assisting other industries in Spring-hill and throughout the maritimes, I think this rug manufacturing industry would not have gone to that province but would have gone to a city like Toronto or Hamilton, or the surrounding area.
Industry itself has not proven its capability to develop in those areas where industry is not now located. I can remember what happened not long ago in the towns of Orillia and Barrie which are probably closer to the large consuming centre than Hamilton. Five years ago in Orillia and Barrie there were people working for 50, 60 or 65 cents an hour. If one listens to what industry says, that should have been all the incentive necessary to bring industry there. It is true that to some extent it did.
I can remember being in Windsor when one of the auxiliary plants of the automobile industry decided to move to Orillia principally because of the lower wage rates in that town. It was not very long until they moved back again to Windsor and relocated their plant there because wages, municipal grants and other incentives commonly used to induce industry to locate in a particular place are not enough to bring about the redevelopment of industry that is necessary in those areas where the need is greatest.
In northern Ontario we are not distant from the market. It is true that industry will say that it cannot go outside of the major consumption areas because the greater portion of their products must be consumed locally or it is not advantageous to them, and I have already indicated that many communities offer incentives that amount to the same advantage in dollars and cents as these industries would have in one of the larger population centres.
